lessons.title: Types of sentences: statements, questions, commands, exclamations; simple and compound
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB — Anglophone primary curriculum, Level III (Classes 5 and 6), English Language — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the four kinds of sentence by their purpose.
Tell a simple sentence from a compound and a complex sentence.
Join short sentences with and, but, so, because.
reviewNotes: Simple/compound/complex are introduced at an elementary level; check how far the Class 6 syllabus goes.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Four kinds of sentence
blocks.md: A **statement** tells us something and ends with a full stop: *I like fufu.* A **question** asks something and ends with a question mark: *Do you like it?* A **command** tells someone to do something: *Eat your food.* An **exclamation** shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark: *How tasty it is!*

blocks.caption: Four kinds of sentence.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: statement (I like fufu), question (Do you like it), command (Eat your food) and exclamation (How tasty it is).

blocks.title: Simple, compound and complex
blocks.md: A **simple** sentence has one main idea: *It rained.* A **compound** sentence joins two main ideas with **and, but, or, so**: *It rained, so we stayed inside.* A **complex** sentence has a main idea and an extra idea that cannot stand alone, joined with words like **because, when, if, although**: *We stayed inside because it rained.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing two sentences with only a comma between them (*It rained, we stayed in*): use a full stop, or add a joining word.
- Starting a sentence with *Because...* and not finishing it (*Because it rained.*). It needs a main idea: *Because it rained, we stayed in.*
- Using both *although* and *but* in one sentence.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Say which kind of sentence each is: (a) Close the door. (b) What a beautiful day!
steps: (a) It tells someone to do something and has no exclamation: it is a command.
(b) It shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark: it is an exclamation.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Join the two sentences with a joining word: It was raining. We stayed inside.
steps: The second idea is a result of the first, so we can use so: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
Or we can use because to make a complex sentence: We stayed inside because it was raining.
blocks.answer: It was raining, so we stayed inside.

lessons.title: Active and passive voice
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB — Anglophone primary curriculum, Level III (Classes 5 and 6), English Language — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Tell an active sentence from a passive sentence.
Change a simple active sentence into the passive and back.
Use the passive correctly in the present, past and future.
reviewNotes: Only the simple present, simple past and simple future are used; check whether the syllabus includes other tenses (present continuous, perfect).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Active and passive
blocks.md: In an **active** sentence the subject does the action: *Ada ate the mango.* In a **passive** sentence the action is done **to** the subject: *The mango was eaten by Ada.* We use the passive when the doer is not important or not known: *The window was broken.*

items.text: The mango was eaten by Ada.

blocks.caption: The same idea in the active and in the passive.
blocks.alt: Two boxes joined by an arrow. The first says Active: Ada ate the mango. The second says Passive: The mango was eaten by Ada.

blocks.title: How to make the passive
blocks.md:
1. Take the **object** of the active sentence: it becomes the new subject.
2. Use the verb **be** in the same tense + the **past participle**: is/are eaten, was/were eaten, will be eaten.
3. Add **by** + the doer (if needed).
Present: *Mama cooks rice.* → *Rice is cooked by Mama.* Past: *Mama cooked rice.* → *Rice was cooked by Mama.* Future: *Mama will cook rice.* → *Rice will be cooked by Mama.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting the verb **be**: *The mango eaten by Ada* is wrong.
- Using the wrong past participle: *was ate* (wrong), *was eaten* (right).
- Not changing the be-verb to match the new subject: *The books was sold* (wrong), *The books were sold* (right).
- Only verbs that take an object can become passive: we cannot say *The boy was slept*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Change to the passive: The farmer planted maize.
steps: The object (maize) becomes the subject.
The verb is in the past: was + planted.
Add by + the doer: by the farmer.
blocks.answer: Maize was planted by the farmer.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Change to the active: The window was broken by the boy.
steps: The doer is the boy: he becomes the subject.
The verb was broken becomes the simple past: broke.
The window is the object.

lessons.title: Direct and indirect (reported) speech
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB — Anglophone primary curriculum, Level III (Classes 5 and 6), English Language — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Tell direct speech from indirect speech.
Change statements, questions and commands into indirect speech.
Change tenses, pronouns and time words correctly.
reviewNotes: Back-shifting rules are given in simplified form; special cases (reporting a general truth, past perfect) are not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Direct and indirect speech
blocks.md: **Direct speech** gives the exact words of a speaker, with quotation marks: *Mama said, “I am cooking rice.”* **Indirect (reported) speech** tells what was said, without quotation marks: *Mama said that she was cooking rice.* In reported speech the tense usually moves one step back: am → was, will → would, can → could, cooks → cooked.

blocks.caption: Words that change in reported speech.
blocks.alt: Eight boxes of word pairs: now becomes then, today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day, yesterday becomes the day before, here becomes there, this becomes that, I and my become he or she, will and can become would and could.

blocks.title: Questions and commands
blocks.md:
- **Statement**: use *that* (or nothing): She said, “I am tired.” → She said (that) she was tired.
- **Question**: use *asked* + **if / whether** (yes-no) or the question word (wh-). Normal word order, no question mark: He asked, “Where do you live?” → He asked where I lived.
- **Command**: use *told / asked* + person + **to**: The teacher said, “Open your books.” → The teacher told us to open our books.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Keeping the question word order: *He asked where did I live* is wrong; say *where I lived*.
- Forgetting to change the pronoun (I → he or she) and the time word (tomorrow → the next day).
- Keeping the quotation marks and the question mark in indirect speech.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Change to indirect speech: Ngu said, “I will come tomorrow.”
steps: Say that. I becomes he, will becomes would.
Tomorrow becomes the next day.
Ngu said that he would come the next day.
blocks.answer: Ngu said that he would come the next day.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Change to indirect speech: Bih asked, “Where is my pen?”
steps: Use asked and the question word where, with statement word order.
My becomes her, is becomes was.
Bih asked where her pen was.
blocks.answer: Bih asked where her pen was.

lessons.title: Conditional sentences
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB — Anglophone primary curriculum, Level III (Classes 5 and 6), English Language — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Form real conditionals (if + present, will) and unreal conditionals (if + past, would).
Use the right verb form after if.
reviewNotes: Third conditional (if + past perfect, would have) is NOT covered; zero conditional is included although the syllabus may not name it.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: What is a conditional?
blocks.md: A **conditional** sentence has an **if**-part (the condition) and a main part (the result). *If it rains, we will stay at home.* The if-part can come first (with a comma) or second (no comma): *We will stay at home if it rains.*

items.text: If it rains, we will stay at home.
If I had a bike, I would ride to school.
If you heat ice, it melts.

blocks.caption: Three kinds of conditional sentence.
blocks.alt: Three boxes. The first shows a real condition: if it rains, we will stay at home. The second shows an unreal one: if I had a bike, I would ride to school. The third shows a fact: if you heat ice, it melts.

blocks.title: Which form?
blocks.md:
- **Real or possible** (it may happen): **if + present simple, will + verb**. *If you study, you will pass.*
- **Unreal or unlikely** (it is not true now): **if + past simple, would + verb**. *If I were a bird, I would fly.* We often say *were* for all persons after if (*if I were*, *if he were*).
- **Always true** (a fact): **if + present, present**. *If you mix red and blue, you get purple.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using will after if: *If it will rain* is wrong; say *If it rains*.
- Mixing the forms: *If I had money, I will buy a bike* is wrong; say *I would buy*.
- Forgetting the comma when the if-part comes first.
- Using *would* in the if-part: *If I would know* is wrong; say *If I knew*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Complete: If it rains tomorrow, we ...... (stay) at home.
steps: Rain tomorrow is possible, so this is a real condition.
The if-part is in the present (rains), so the result takes will + verb.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Complete: If I ...... (be) a bird, I would fly over Mount Cameroon.
steps: A person cannot be a bird, so this is unreal.
The if-part is in the past, and we use were: if I were a bird.

exercises.explanation: For example: is cooked, was written.

exercises.prompt: The passive of 'They will build a bridge' is...
